speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Since the federal government should establish a long term policy to protect and stabilize the production of industrial milk, since this important industry should at least enjoy the same increase in income as other fields of activity to compensate for the cost of living instead of having their income reduced by some 20 per cent this year, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That, before the implementation of the government dairy policies for 1976-77, this House discuss immediately the necessity of respecting established quotas and having adequate measures to guarantee decent incomes which would at least take production costs into account and put a stop to the ever growing discouragement felt by those producers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister acknowledged that he had the right to know the conversations between ministers that may involve any impropriety. On Monday, as indicated at page 11788 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
I have not only the word of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs but also the public statement of the Minister of Public Works that he-

March 17, 1976
Oral Questions
Being the Minister of Public Works.
-did this-
Being the intervention.
-was not pushed to do it by anyone and that he-
The Minister of Public Works.
-took full responsibility.
My question is this. In light of the admission yesterday by the former minister, that he asked the Minister of Public Works to intervene, did the Prime Minister know about that request for intervention before Monday of this week? If not, when did he learn of that request for intervention?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Mr. Ouellet told me about that precise request he made to the minister on Monday of this week.

subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question? The Prime Minister indicated that he conversed with the ministers involved. He now suggests that his conversations with the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs did not reveal that information, that is, that the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs had made the request of the Minister of Public Works. Just so that I can be clear, is the Prime Minister telling the House that for almost two weeks after Mr. Justice Mackay made his allegation, an allegation now clearly vindicated, that he, the Prime Minister, did not ask the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs if he had requested that intervention by the Minister of Public Works?

subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. That is right. I got the answer from the minister on Monday, the day before yesterday, and I explained to the House yesterday why that was my line of conduct. As soon as Justice Mackay's letters were published or made public in the press, I wanted to, and did, ascertain from both ministers whether they had done anything which might be interpreted as illegally interfering with the court or impeding the course of justice. I got that assurance from them. Because I wanted to make sure that that was not a one-sided assurance, we followed the course which the Minister of Justice took, of asking the point of view of the courts on this matter: did they feel there had been any illegal interference. Until I had that judgment or assessment from Chief Justice Des-chenes on Thursday night, I did not attempt to know exactly, in all details, what went on between the two ministers.

subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister, as the only person responsible for the propriety of conduct of ministers, telling the House that the only question he put to the two ministers involved-and any others whom we do not know about but who might have been involved- was whether they thought they had been involved in an illegality? Did he ask whether they thought they had been involved in an illegality? Is that the only question he put to them?

subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I just answered that. I asked if there had been an illegality, or an improper attempt to interfere with the course of justice, or to influence a

decision, and so on. That was my concern. I wanted to make sure that there had been no attempt to interfere with the course of justice in any way which would be improper, illegal or considered unacceptable.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: Or which could be considered as wrongdoing.

subsubtopic: DATE ON WHICH PRIME MINISTER KNEW OF MR. OUELLET'S REQUEST OF MR. DRURY TO CALL JUDGE HUGESSEN
speechtext: I got their answers and I wanted to hear from the chief justice what the point of view of the courts was on this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS TO ASCERTAIN FACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this I find incredible. Will the Prime Minister, as the person responsible for the propriety of conduct of ministers, tell the House how he felt he had the right to sit back and wait for the courts to report on the matter, without asking detailed questions as to whether the allegations raised by Mr. Justice Mackay were in fact the case? What right did he have to sit back and avoid facing his ministers with the question as to what, precisely, they had done?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS TO ASCERTAIN FACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I felt that I had not only the right; I had the duty not to delve into this question, as it might have been-

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS TO ASCERTAIN FACTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS TO ASCERTAIN FACTS
speechtext: -completely irrelevant to the allegations of Justice Mackay. The allegations of Justice Mackay were to the effect that there had been serious interference with the course of justice. I wanted to assure myself, from the ministers, that this was not the case. I did assume myself from the ministers that that was not the case. I even had the assurance it was not illegal and not improper. Mr. Drury, obviously, would not have done something he believed to be improper. I had his version of it and Mr. Ouellet's version. According to both their versions, there had not only been no illegality; there had been no impropriety. Obviously, Justice Deschenes and Justice Hugessen do not share that point of view. However, I prefer to get it from them rather than to just hear from Justice Mackay. It seems to be perfectly in order.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER TYPE OF APPROACH TO JUDICIARY BY MR. DRURY WILL BE PROHIBITED
INQUIRY WHETHER TYPE OF APPROACH TO JUDICIARY BY MR. DRURY WILL BE PROHIBITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Minister of Public Works stated:
-I think the hon. gentleman would agree that a case before the courts in which the court itself appeared to be of the parties and a member of the executive being the other, carried out a full-scale battle based on a possible misunderstanding at the outset, would be an unnecessary confrontation, and any conflict based on this misunderstanding appears to me to be inappropriate and useless. It is the job of a public official to avoid this kind of thing if that can be done, and that is what I was seeking to do.
Will the Prime Minister assure us that he recognizes that that statement itself constitutes evidence of an attempt to influence the outcome of a court proceeding and, because
March 17, 1976

of the new so-called code of ethics, will be proscribed in the future?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER TYPE OF APPROACH TO JUDICIARY BY MR. DRURY WILL BE PROHIBITED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as far as the code of ethics is concerned, I enunciated quite clearly on Friday rules which would indicate that in the future I do not expect that course to be followed. I have done that because it has been judged improper, because there has been an apology and so on. However, I must state, and I believe this is also Justice Hugessen's view, that the demarche of the Minister of Public Works was not viewed as something dishonourable. It was explained by Justice Hugessen on the contrary as something honourable, an effort by the executive and the judicial arm-

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER TYPE OF APPROACH TO JUDICIARY BY MR. DRURY WILL BE PROHIBITED
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER TYPE OF APPROACH TO JUDICIARY BY MR. DRURY WILL BE PROHIBITED
speechtext: Hon. members can just refer to what Justice Hugessen said in his report to Chief Justice Des-chenes. He said he was convinced that the Minister of Public Works' initative was based on a desire to avoid a confrontation. To me, there is nothing dishonourable in that.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER TYPE OF APPROACH TO JUDICIARY BY MR. DRURY WILL BE PROHIBITED

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In none of the letters released to the press two weeks ago today was there any reference to illegal behaviour by any minister. Will the Prime Minister explain why he did not put the direct non-legal question to the ministers about whom allegations had been made, to the Minister of Public Works on the one hand "Did you or did you not intervene with the judge on behalf of the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs" and to that minister, "Did you or did you not ask the Minister of Public Works to intervene on your behalf".

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw in those letters, as did members opposite, that in fact the Minister of Public Works had spoken to Justice Hugessen. This was alleged by Justice Mackay. Naturally, I asked the Minister of Public Works was this so, what was he trying to do and was he trying to do something improper, as Justice Mackay alleged he was interfering in the course of justice. I think that is the expression used by Justice Mackay. I wanted to assure myself that in the view of the Minister of Public Works, he was not trying to obtain a different or better decision, but trying to make sure that any conflict between an individual and the courts, a confrontation as was just described in the previous question, would be avoided, if possible.
At that stage, I addressed myself to the Minister of Public Works, since he was mentioned in Justice Mackay's letter. I also addressed myself to the Minister of National Health and Welfare because he too was mentioned in the letter, even though his interventions in 1970 were not made as a minister, but as an official.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext:
It took some time.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: Yes, it took some time. I think that is very relevant. As the hon. member looks at the dossier, he might ask himself why Justice Mackay took that length of time to be indignant about it.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: If the hon. member looks at the dossier he might ask himself why Justice Mackay took that length of time to become indignant about it.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: I addressed myself to the third minister who was brought into question by Mr. Justice Mackay, the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs. I must confess I do not remember asking questions immediately of the minister of consumer and corporate affairs. I am sorry the President of the Treasury Board was the third one. Mr. Justice Mackay does not mention the hon. member for Papineau except in passing, as he mentioned my name in a way in which hon. members have been, I guess, gracious enough or wise enough not even to refer to. I remember that the hon. member for Papineau had indeed talked to me and presumably asked advice of many other colleagues and friends at the time of his trial. But his name was not brought into play by Mr. Justice Mackay in any improper way. I do not remember whether in those days I asked anything further of the hon. member for Papineau.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: I must say, and I make this comment most seriously, that I find the Prime Minister's answer extraordinary. If, as I understand it, the Prime Minister had posed a direct question two weeks ago to the three ministers most directly involved and got honest and direct answers, even the information which has since been published, does the right hon. gentleman not realize that no reference for a report need have been made to the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec? Such a reference would not have been necessary had he obtained that information directly and conveyed it honestly to the House.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: I reported to the House at the time that I had asked the question directly and I had the opinion of the ministers that they had not done anything illegal, that they had not done anything which, in their minds, appeared to be even improper. Hon. members heard the President of the Treasury Board explain the circumstances under which he made a phone call. He did not tell me he had done something improper. He felt at the time he was doing his duty to his electorate. The courts have a different opinion and that is why I issued the rules. The same applies to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and to the Minister of Public Works. It would be unthinkable that they would do something deliberately which they knew would be improper and which would get them into trouble with the judge.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: Oh!

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext:
Members opposite do not have to take my word for it. They just have to take what Justice Hugessen himself sees as the reason for the intervention by the Minister of Public Works; he says he thinks it was done

March 17, 1976

with the best of intentions. I believe the judge uses the same expression in reference to the Minister of National Health and Welfare; he says he did it for reasons of state and not for personal advantage. So when I got this kind of answer from the ministers I took it at face value-and this is the value which the judges themselves are putting on it.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: With specific reference to the hon. member for Papineau, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether or not he put the following direct question to that minister: Did you urge the Minister of Public Works to intervene with the judge on your behalf? If the right hon. gentleman did not ask that question, I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman this: did he not leave the House for two weeks with the impression that that question had been posed, and, consequently, does he not leave his office open to the very serious charge that there has been two weeks of attempted cover-up concerning this matter?

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: I have no doubt in my mind that that is the charge the hon. member is attempting to establish. But he has my answers during those two weeks in which I made it quite clear that I asked the ministers whether they had acted illegally or improperly. Having ascertained from them that they had not-

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: In their judgment.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES

speechtext: Not in your judgment.

subtopic: REASON PRIME MINISTER DID NOT QUESTION MINISTERS ABOUT INTERVENTION WITH JUDGES
speechtext: Not in my judgment, Mr. Speaker. But it is because our judgment might conceivably be put in doubt by the other side that I found it fit and proper to ask the courts, through the Minister of Justice, what was their version of the facts. Until that was obtained I was satisfied with the response of my ministers, and as I indicated to the House yesterday I did not feel that I had, to use the words that have been used, the right and duty to get into all aspects of this question. So far as conversations between ministers having anything to do with illegality or even, in their view, impropriety, I do not feel I have a right to know every detail.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY TO DETERMINE IF JUDGES INTERFERED WITH GOVERNMENT
REQUEST FOR INQUIRY TO DETERMINE IF JUDGES INTERFERED WITH GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to direct a question to the Prime Minister.
Since the official opposition as well as the NDP are requesting an inquiry into the behaviour of two cabinet ministers in order to clear this whole matter, and we share their opinion, does the Prime Minister believe that such an inquiry would help unclog the business of the House and does he not also think that it would be advisable in conducting this inquiry to have certain judges appear before the same committee to determine precisely whether there has been any interference from them into the affairs of ministers or government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY TO DETERMINE IF JUDGES INTERFERED WITH GOVERNMENT
speechtext: The leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada is referring to one of the difficulties I pointed out yesterday in the House. He is indeed asking the question, as I did myself in the House, whether an inquiry might be made and must be made by Parliament, that is the legislative branch of the government, on the conduct of the judges. Do we have the right to summon them here to answer on their conduct? The hon. member seems to think so. Anyway, I heard someone say yes. I do not think this is so sure, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think that it is sure either that judges would feel compelled to answer the call of Parliament to appear before us and testify, unless it is under the impeachment procedure. What seems rather strange to me in all this, since now the facts are known and those arguments explained, is that hon. members in the opposition keep complaining about interference by the executive with the judiciary, while they are quite in a hurry to urge interference by the legislative with the judiciary. This does not seem very consistent.

SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO LEARN CONVERSATION WITH MR. TURNER CONCERNING INTERVENTION WITH JUDGE-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext: Judges have certainly appeared before public inquiries before, Mr. Speaker, but on a different subject completely may I address my question to the Prime Minister.

speechtext: Not so.

speechtext: Give an example.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO LEARN CONVERSATION WITH MR. TURNER CONCERNING INTERVENTION WITH JUDGE-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext: I can give an example if hon. members want: a former justice, Mr. Justice Landreville for one. In any event Mr. Turner, the former minister of justice told a television reporter on Monday that he learned a lot because he "keeps his mouth shut". Now that the Prime Minister concedes that the conversations related to at least an act of impropriety, has the Prime Minister attempted to pry his version of these events out of Mr. Turner?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO LEARN CONVERSATION WITH MR. TURNER CONCERNING INTERVENTION WITH JUDGE-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the question must have been asked in jest. Mr. Turner was no longer a member of the cabinet when the contempt of court proceedings were initiated. When I say that conversations between private individuals as far as I am concerned are privileged, and that I have no right to pry into them, surely that applies also to the former Minister of Justice and former finance minister.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONTENT OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR OUELLET AND MR. DRURY CONCERNING INTERVENTION WITH JUDGE
REQUEST FOR CONTENT OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR OUELLET AND MR. DRURY CONCERNING INTERVENTION WITH JUDGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are getting information in little bits and pieces and having to pry them out. I should like to put this question to the Prime Minister which might shorten this whole problem. Yesterday the Prime Minister told the House that "parliament also has that right" which he possesses to examine conversations between ministers "when there is any wrongdoing". He went on to state that on the part of the Minister of Public Works there was in fact "an element of wrongdoing". This being the case, is the Prime Minister now prepared to inform the House of the exact nature of the conversations between the Minister of Public Works and the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs? If we get these facts then surely we will know where we stand.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONTENT OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR OUELLET AND MR. DRURY CONCERNING INTERVENTION WITH JUDGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs stated what he had asked the Minister of Public Works. Therefore, the facts are now before the House. They were not before the House until then because, and I repeat, we were waiting for Mr. Justice Deschenes' view of those facts. It was our intention to get the view and the appreciation of the courts on what had happened. Obviously, the actors involved on this side had not done anything which they then considered to be improper. If the courts judged differently then we were bound to take into consideration their assessment of it, and it is because of that that I enunciated new rules on Friday. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the facts the opposition has been trying to get have been made known in so far as they were relevant to this case. If the hon. member is interested in gossip or irrelevant things which might have been said between those two ministers or any others he will not get them from me and I hope he will not get them from the others. Similarly with a court of inquiry, it would only ask questions which are relevant to some form of misconduct.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CONTENT OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR OUELLET AND MR. DRURY CONCERNING INTERVENTION WITH JUDGE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Finance. I want to thank him for sending the brief over to me. speechtext:
1.	How many fisheries guardians were employed in the Province of Newfoundland in (a) 1975 (b) 1974 (c) 1973 (d) 1972 (e) 1971 (f) 1970?
2.	What was their term of employment?
3.	Are they eligible for unemployment insurance benefits after termination of their employment and, if so, has any consideration been given to setting up familiarization courses into anti-pollution measures or anti-poaching measures, rather than laying them off?
4.	Has any consideration been given to providing instruction to fisheries guardians in the use of firearms and to allow them to carry firearms while on duty?
5.	Is compensation provided for meals when fisheries guardians are away from their home base on duty and, if so (a) in what amount (b) for how long has such meal allowance been in existence?
6.	What is the meal allowance for (a) fisheries wardens (b) all fisheries officials when away from their home base?
7.	Has there been an increase in poaching activity in the Atlantic Region and, if so, what measures have been taken by the Department of the Environment to prevent poaching?
8.	How much money under the 1976-77 estimates has been allocated to increase the number of fisheries wardens and guardians?
9.	Has any consideration been given, on the basis of the cost of living increase, to increasing the meal allowance for fisheries guardians and, if not, for what reason?
10.	Have any studies been carried out to assess the number of fisheries wardens and/or guardians required to provide adequate surveillance measures in the Province of Newfoundland and (a) if so, what were the findings (b) if not, for what reason?
11 By province, how many poachers have been apprehended in the Atlantic Region in (a) 1970 (b) 1971 (c) 1972 (d) 1973 (e) 1974 (f) 1975?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: FISHERIES GUARDIANS-ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
1. The
number of fisheries guardians employed in Newfoundland for the years 1975 to 1970 inclusive are as follows: (a) 1975: 169; (b) 1974: 185; (c) 1973: 185; (d) 1972: 186; (e) 1971: 151; (f) 1970: 105.
2.	The term of employment normally varies between a minimum of three months to a maximum of five months depending on the area and the requirements of the particular position.
3.	Guardians are eligible for Unemployment Insurance Benefits if they have met the required number of contributory weeks. Familiarization courses have not been considered for fisheries guardians on terrr;"ation of their employment as funds are not available for this purpose and in addition the turnover in these employees is such that it would be impractical.
4.	Consideration has not been given to providing instruction to fisheries guardians in the use of firearms as it is not deemed to be necessary nor would it be practical in view of the length of the employment period and the annual turnover in staff.
5.	(a) Meal allowances are provided for fisheries guardians away from their home base on duty in accordance with the rates laid down by the Treasury Board Travel Regulations, (b) This allowance has been applied since its inception.
6.	Meal allowance for all fisheries staff when away from their home base on duty are at the rates provided under the Treasury Board Travel Regulations.
7.	An assessment of overall poaching activity can at best only provide an estimate of the level of this activity. In
March 17, 1976

Newfoundland for the years 1970-1974 there was very little change in the pattern or level of illegal fishing but during 1975 there was a marked increase. For the most part this was due to low water conditions and the fact that most of the rivers in that province were closed during the salmon angling season. Throughout the Atlantic area poaching usually develops into a major problem in particular locations and this requires the deployment of additional staff during these critical periods. Such temporary transfers of staff are the principal measures used to control particular problems and are found to be quite effective.
8.	No additional funds have been allocated in the 1976-77 estimates to increase the number of fisheries wardens and guardians and it is most unlikely that there will be any change in this regard in view of the budgetary constraints that are being applied generally.
9.	Treasury Board reviews meal allowance rates on a regular basis and adjusts them accordingly to compensate for changes in the cost of living.
10.	The requirements in terms of staff to provide an adequate enforcement and surveillance capability throughout Newfoundland are constantly under review. During 1975 a total of 65 fishery wardens and 169 fishery guardians were employed. Although conditions experienced in 1975 were probably extreme, a modest increase in staff for both classes of employee may be necessary and will be considered in planning for future staff requirements.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It is a pleasure to be able to resume the normal business of the House and discuss this very important bill. In the first few minutes that I had in addressing myself to this matter, I made a point that I think has constantly to be made since members of the opposition tend to have great difficulty dealing with what the bill proposes to do. I mentioned that the bill deals only with medical care. It does not deal with hospital care. It deals with a number of other things associated with medical care as distinct from hospital care.
The bill proposes for the first year it would begin, on April 1, 1976, that the increase in the federal allotment to the provinces for this particular item would not exceed 13 per cent, in the second year would not exceed 11 per cent, and in the third year would be negotiated but probably would be, I understand, in the area of 10 percent. This is what the bill does, and it does this under the circumstances of the anti-inflation program that now exists. We believe, with a good deal of reason, that the circumstances are favourable and we can expect an 8.5 per cent increase in the coming year in terms of cost of living as opposed to the 13 per cent increase in terms of medical costs allowed. In the second year we hope it will be down to 6 per cent as opposed to the 11 per cent, and so on. We think there is a good deal of generosity and extra money involved in this program and that we are justified in making these limitations.
I dealt very briefly with the contribution of the NDP in the area of medical care. I congratulated them for their many years of concern and effort toward achieving medical care in this country. They were not the only ones who were concerned, but I have spoken to them about this and I did congratulate them. I must also indicate that had the progressives in this country been in the Liberal party rather than off in the corner, the 40 years of effort might have enjoyed success considerably earlier. I would also grant that under any given circumstances an idea does not happen until its time has arrived.
Let me continue my thoughts on a few points which I do not recall having been mentioned in this debate in terms of

the position of the NDP and the Conservatives. What I have in mind is the basic difference existing in the House of Commons between this government and the opposition in respect of our relationship with the provinces. It is my personal belief that we, as the government, possibly because we have been in power longer in this century-

speechtext: Too long.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
-have a far stronger federal, national position. I think this was the position of the Tory party when it was in power in the last century. The NDP and the Tory parties have become very closely related to the governments of the various provinces and I would suspect they are very strongly representing ultimate provincial interests when they oppose this bill. There is an interesting conflict. I do not mean there is a confrontation between the provinces and the federal government or that we want it to be this way. Our position, as the government in power, has to be one of responsibility and one that primarily concerns Canadians. It must be a position which recognizes that Canada is not just the sum of its provinces.
Let me deal with the Conservative viewpoint on this particular bill. My first area of comment relates to the question: Do we need medicare? I find it very difficult to understand why eight or ten years after the fact this question has arisen. I find it difficult to accept the suggestion that medicare was shoved down our throats. I am convinced, as I was convinced 20 years ago, that this kind of medicare program is absolutely essential. I was convinced of this more than anything else perhaps, by an event that happened in our family in the late 1950s.
A very close member of the family, a remarkable woman, spent her life raising a large family. She worked very hard for years and years. One thing, she wanted in her life above all else was that when she died there would be no bills to pay. She wanted to be self-sustaining. She bought into a private medical scheme and paid the premiums for nine years. It was a scheme offered by one of the largest companies, not a fly-by-night operation. She participated in this scheme which she felt would look after her, medically, so long as she kept up the premiums. What happened? I ask this question because I think the answer is important in terms of the need for medicare. She became ill with cancer and went into the hospital. After her having one operation, this company-one of the largest in the world in this field-sent a notice that it would no longer accept premiums from her to cover any illness in respect of cancer. She was never told about this. We did not have the heart to tell her that, after paying the premiums for all those years, she was not covered. We looked after the whole thing from then on, and she lived for only six months.
This was a very dramatic event in our family, following which the family and all our friends realized how badly we needed a medical care scheme. There were some good schemes in existence. PSI was one, but it did not cover everyone, at least in the province of Ontario. It covered a number of groups, but a large proportion of the people in the province did not belong to those groups. These are some of the reasons that lead me to believe we need medicare, and that is why this bill should be supported.

I could go on at some length in this regard, but I should now like to deal with the financial side of the matter. I find it very difficult to understand why the Conservative party is acting in what I consider to be a very irresponsible way in respect of this particular bill. This leads me to wonder if the beliefs of that party are sound or deep. We have now reached the fourteenth or fifteenth day of debate on this bill and we are still at second reading stage. The sole purpose of the bill is to limit medical expenses.
In the last few days members of the Conservative party have had their minds on other things, but during this session those members have been criticizing the government for its huge deficits and expenditures. They have continued to insist that we must cut back. I find their position on this bill very difficult to understand. Let us consider some government expenditures in order to determine why this is one area in which we must cut back or at least limit increases in spending. Let me take the fiscal years 1974-75 and 1975-76. In 1974-75, out of a total of $30 billion this government spent $8.6 billion on the whole operation of government, including the armed forces, all the departments and the public service. The balance of $22 billion was in the form of transfer payments to persons, provinces and corporations for subsidies, and so on.
This money went to persons in the form of old age pensions and unemployment insurance. It went to paying off the debt. These were transfers to people, organizations, provinces and other levels of government. Over two-thirds of the total amount was spent in the form of transfer payments; a very large portion was in transfer payments to the provinces. This amounted to $6.5 billion in 1974-75.
Let us look at 1975-76. In that year we went from $8.6 billion to $9.5 billion in respect of the total cost of the operation of the federal government, including the public service, defence and the whole bit. However, in the same period, while there was an increase of about $.9 billion, the cost of the transfer payments increased in excess of $4 billion: it went up to $26 billion. As a matter of fact, between those two periods the total expenditures of the federal government increased by 16.8 per cent. But of that 16.8 per cent increase between 1974-75 and 1975-76, only 2.8 percentage points were for the operation of the government, and 14 percentage points were in the transfer area. We can see from that, with a little calculation, that the transfer area was increasing between those two years at three times the rate of the increase in the operation of the government.

speechtext: Do you know why?

speechtext:
I think I have some ideas. If the hon. member would like to tell us, he can. The point is that it is extremely significant that the transfer costs are increasing at three times the increase in the operational costs of the government. So I think we must look at these transfer costs because they represent a large proportion of the cost.
Although I have some experience in this regard I have difficulty understanding the opposition to this bill in terms of the cost-sharing programs. The Conservative party, but not the New Democratic Party to the same extent, constantly talk about cutting back. Anyone who
Medical Care Act
has any experience-and I, as principal of a high school for many years, have experience in this regard-with costsharing formulas realizes that if you are the person spending the money, you trigger the amount spent.
I have been involved in cost-sharing arrangements where we put up 10 per cent and the other government put up 90 per cent. For putting up 10 per cent we got back a lot of money. That is the kind of thing that happens in costsharing. In order to make cost-sharing work with any degree of equity, I think it is necessary to have a ceiling. This is what is being done by this bill. A ceiling of 13 percentage points is being placed on the amount the federal government will give to the provinces for this particular program. This does not mean that the provinces cannot spend more. I think this is a necessary factor in cost-sharing. I think this can be a very dangerous arrangement when there is no recourse on the part of the one government, in this case the federal government, in terms of the amount it would have to put up. So if the Tory party is genuinely concerned about cutting back government expenditures, I think it must look at some of these cost-sharing arrangements.
I suggest to the Conservative party that we have made some attempt to cut back. We have not done all we could- there is no question about that-but we have done a significant amount in the area dealing with the operations: we have cut well over $1 billion from that. I am not particularly the type of person who argues that government expenditures essentially are a bad thing. As a matter of fact, even a government deficit would create jobs and promote growth in the country. However, if one wants to cut, I believe one must look at the area of the transfer of funds because this is where the money is. No one denies there is fat in the other areas, but this is the main area.
I have heard the suggestion in the House that one area we could cut is family allowances. We have done something in this regard in the form of indexing family allowances. The cutting of family allowances, in the sense of applying a means test, is a dangerous business. Family allowances, even for those who are fairly affluent in our society, represent an important thing for the family. I know there are very many people in our society, housewives, and so on, who consider this cheque to be very important, not just because they need the money but because it is not in the name of their husband or anyone else and it is theirs to spend as they see fit. That is a very important element. When one refers to the cutting of family allowances, that should be taken into account. If family allowances were to be cut or placed strictly on the basis of a means test, there might be a saving of half a million dollars, but this would affect many families because the family allowance cheque is an essential ingredient for any family, and not simply because the money is needed. So it seems to me we must look at many other areas.
I have not heard suggestions about how the cuts should be made; I have only heard suggestions that there should be cuts. We have not had any suggestions along this line from the opposition, because if the opposition were to say that there should be cuts here or there, then they would be taking the responsibility for those cuts and the public would hold them responsible. So when one is in the opposi-

tion, one does not say where the cuts should be, so the opposition does not have to take the responsibility. I challenge members of the opposition to say where they would cut significantly. I am not talking about a bit of fat here and there. I know that has to be done, but where can these cuts be made significantly? I suggest this is one of the areas we must move into.
We have made sure that the increases in medical care grants from the federal government over the years since the scheme has been in effect have been far greater than some inflationary increases and gross national product increases because it was important to improve medical care. So we let this happen. We have allowed no limits, because we felt it was worth while. Now the government says it must do some cutting and that there must be a limit. Things have been left up to this point. Health costs have been mounting at a tremendous rate. We know we have to impose a ceiling, and it has been set at 13 per cent for the next fiscal year. This seems like a reasonable situation. As I said earlier, 13 per cent is reasonable if during the fiscal year there is only an 8 per cent or an 8.5 per cent increase in the cost of living.
The increase is still greater than the total of the inflation in the dollar and the total of the increase in the gross national product. I think at this particular point there is some real justification for this kind of limitation. It is not a cut. We are not going to spend less; we are going to spend more than we did last year. However, we have a limit to a cost-sharing program whereby no one can spend so much money and trigger a very large increase on the part of the federal government. The cost-sharing areas have given us much trouble over the years, and I think this is a useful way of approaching this particular problem.
I should like to conclude by repeating something I said earlier. At first I was talking about the NDP, but now I shall refer to the Tory party. I believe the Tory party believes this country is the sum of its provinces and, rightly so, they have very close relations with the provinces. They have not been in power nationally for any significant period in this century, so therefore their ties are with their provincial governments, and rightly so, because there are four Tory provincial governments in this country and I am sure hon. members opposite have good relations with those governments.
Therefore, I believe some of the opposition to this bill stems partly from the support these federal members want to extend to their provinces, and rightly so. But I plead with hon. members to recognize that this country is something much more than the sum of the ten provinces. We in this House must deal with the good of the whole country, and this kind of limitation of cost-sharing arrangements is the one way in which we can significantly reduce federal government spending.

I detected from the remarks of the hon. member who spoke previously, indirectly and directly, one of the reasons this country is in a great deal of trouble today. He articulated the kind of principles of federalism which are so often articulated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the kind of view about Canada today which sort of wishes that we were not really a federal union at all, that we could just sweep the provinces under the carpet and pretend they do not exist or that we can confront them.
I believe one of the reasons this country is so divided today is that Ottawa has attempted, by confronting the provinces in the last eight years, to sweep regional and provincial differences under the carpet in an attempt to impose a monolithic uniformity on Canadian federalism. That is just not the kind of country we have. What the hon. member has just articulated is the kind of wishful thinking articulated by doctrinaire Liberals in the last eight years which has divided this country as it has never been divided. You cannot articulate an "either/or" debate. Any Canadian prime minister, be he Progressive Conservative or Liberal, has to defend and define a strong federal cause. But at the same time, whether the hon. member likes it or not, there are provinces in this country which must be co-operated with and worked with-not confronted.
I am very interested in the question of escalating costs vis-a-vis joint programs. I know why there are escalating costs vis-a-vis joint programs. It is because since World War II successive Liberal governments, without truly consulting with the provinces, unilaterally have imposed programs. Some of them have been very good programs in principle-medicare is one of them-but the government imposes programs without truly-I underline the word "truly"-consulting the provinces, working with them and listening to them. speechtext:
It has always been thus. The poor are very often the least capable of being good lobbyists, so what happens? When there are obvious cuts to be made in the billions of dollars worth of government expenditure, they get it in the neck every time. The low income people who were meant to be served by decent medical and health care services are the ones who suffer.
(Mr. Paproski.]
It is passing strange to me, Mr. Speaker, that a government that has seen expenditures go from $10 billion to $36 billion a year, with the economy on its knees, does not even generate enough growth in the private sector to get new programs going, let alone sustain one passed by the Pearson administration. They look around for things to cut and they cut medicare, the delivery of medical and health care service to people at the grass roots level. That is a wonder to me. Instead of listening to the voice of the people on the floor of the House, where is the minister? He is with the bureaucrats in an ivory tower. A cut here and a cut there: they do not listen to the silent poor and the grass roots people because they are poorer lobbyists. They say, "We are going to cut medicare." That is wonderful!
At a time in Canadian history when we should be talking about leading the world in the delivery of medical and health care services, what are these fellows doing? They are cutting back on services. Just ask anybody in the medical and health care world. After eight years of Trudeau administration, medical and health care services have slipped slowly but surely from excellence to mediocrity and if we go any longer with this administration they are going to be very poor. Ask anyone. Are hon. members opposite so blindly partisan that they do not listen? The paramedical workers and the medical health care service people can tell you things have slipped from excellence to mediocrity. Now we are faced with a cut in services.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the economy has been so mismanaged by this government that there has not been enough room in the private sector not only to inaugurate new and imaginative programs but to sustain existing ones. It is worth repeating that government expenditures rose from $10 billion to $36 billion annually. How did the government devise the formula for controlling costs? It has never explained this to the House or to the provinces. Apparently it pulled the formula out of thin air. It is an arbitrary formula, so complicated that no backbencher or minister understands it. How can the provinces understand this mishmash of nonsense, this so-called formula for controlling medical care expenses? The government is obligated to explain to the provinces, before confronting them with a fait accompli, how it evolved its cost-sharing formulas. After all, it was done without consultation.
Consider the history of medicare. Nobody likes saying, "I told you so." I do not. Most of us want to see good programs working. Hon. members who were here during the 1960s when medicare was brought in do not like saying, "I told you so." In those days the government's position was that you were either for medicare or against it. It would not accept amendments hon. members on my side suggested. When we suggested amendments which would have made medicare work better, we were accused of being against the program.
Those on my side of the House who were in touch with the grass roots knew that the people of the country were in accord with the principle of medicare. The Liberals adopt a "holier than thou" attitude as if they only are favoured in the sight of God. They think that only they supported the principle of medicare. They are wrong. We, too, sincerely believed in the principle of medicare. Because we suggested amendments to the original bill which would take into
March 17, 1976

account the history, priorities and politics of different provinces, we were accused of being against medicare. Now the chickens have come home to roost.
Although we supported the principle of universal medicare, we recognized the different needs of the provinces. We took into account the needs of Saskatchewan which had begun a medicare program of its own. Manitoba had begun a group program. The needs of Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces were different. We knew this. But did the federal authority consult the provinces? No. It said to the provinces, "If you don't like it, lump it." Ten years later it says to the provinces, "Now we shall control costs our way, and that is that." That is not my idea of federalism. Does the hon. member who preceded me support that kind of federalism?
How is medicare in Canada working? Let me draw an analogy. Let us suppose that the people of a town are starving and have not enough money with which to buy bread. The town council, in its wisdom, votes money with which the people can buy bread. Unfortunately, the town council has not telephoned the bakery to discover if the bakery can supply the bread. The upshot is that although it voted the starving town dwellers money with which to buy bread, they starve simply because the council did not make sure that the bakery had bread to sell.
That illustrates what has happened to medicare. Like so many joint federal-provincial programs, it is neither fish, fowl nor fair weather. Medicare is merely a means for paying for non-existent services. Medical service is not available in many rural communities, towns and villages. Sometimes it is not accessible to people living in the inner part of cities. The program was designed to help these very people, and it failed. The government provided money for a service which is just not there. I know my analogy is not complete, but it will do. Until the government takes account of the priorities of the provinces and their ability to provide humane, decent medical service, until it consults with the provinces to make sure that medical personnel and facilities are available, medicare for many will be a cruel hoax.
The government did not consult the provinces to discover if there were facilities and personnel for implementing medicare. Medicare has become a means for transferring money and paying for non-existent services. In the 1950s people in public life thought that if your heart was in the right place and you threw enough money at a problem, it would correct itself overnight. That attitude will not work in the 1970s and 1980s. The government must listen to the provinces and work with them.
In many ways, our medicare program combines the worst features of private enterprise and socialism. Because you throw taxpayers' dollars at a problem does not mean it will go away. The government set up a joint program it called medicare. It is a program involving transfer payments and in many ways is typical of some of the worst joint programs forced on the provinces since the Second World War. Why, Mr. Speaker? The government did not consult the provinces. It set no limits, did no real planning. If it planned with the provinces, why are we in the present mess? The government wants to make the provinces responsible for the program. Why should the provinces be responsible when initially the government would not
Medical Care Act
listen to the provinces, paid no heed to their priorities and imposed, unilaterally, this inflexible program?
Now, ten years later, it comes to the House and says, "We broke the bank." What nonsense! Anyone who suggests that we can discuss medicare without discussing at the same time hospital insurance is talking nonsense. That is pure bunkum. If that is their attitude, small wonder our medical care programs are in disarray. You cannot approach medicare as if it were in a vacuum. You must consider the total package of medical care services.
What is happening in Canada? I hope I am being nonpartisan. At the very time we ought to consider how to maintain and improve one of the best health care services in the world, we are cutting medical research. Talk to health researchers in this country. They do not know what to do. Many of the world's leading research programs have been scrapped. Needed services are being scrapped. Why? The government turns a deaf ear to requests for consultation with provinces in this area as well.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) can meet with his officials to the end of time trying to devise formulas to control costs. However, until the plant and personnel are made ready, we will really be whistling in the dark. I remember speaking to the then minister of national health and welfare when we were initially passing medicare. As the debate went on I asked to what extent, in the provinces and municipalities, the plant and personnel were ready. She said, "Not really at all, but if we wait for it to be ready, we will wait forever." I, and most other people, agreed that we could not hold back this universal program called medicare until the plant and personnel were ready. However, that is not an excuse to have done relatively nothing with the provinces in the past ten years in terms of planning and building up plant and personnel.
What do we in Canada have compared to other countries in the western world? In the province of Quebec we have the Castonguay report. It is probably one of the best reports in the world vis-a-vis the delivery of medical and health care services. I often wonder if the minister has read it. What about the 1970 Ontario royal commission report on the healing arts? Like the Castonguay report, it is one of the greatest documents of all time on the delivery of medical and health care services. What about our governmental experience in Saskatchewan years and years ago in terms of initiating a public health measure? We could learn from that. But does this government ever learn from anything? In the area of research and Dr. Wilder Penfield, 12 years ago we were recognized all over the world as being excellent. We have slipped worldwide from excellent to mediocre because of this government's insistence that it knows it all and that the people at the local level do not know anything.
If you read these reports, they are far flung. Has there been any real discussion with the provinces about ambulatory care networks, the proper training of paramedical workers? I am looking at the Ontario example of emergency services, community clinics and emphasis on preventive medicine, home care, general clinics and regional responsibilities that hospitals should take in terms of the health

care needs of a total community in the area of curative and preventive medicine.
A cursory reading of these reports shows, like any other business, how to save money, not spend money. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), when he was minister of national health and welfare, reiterated the need for national standards vis-a-vis hospital regionalization where the community hospital would be the hub in the community in respect of total health care services and meeting the needs of the community. Has the minister read these things? Is he aware of them? Is the federal government going to continue to confront the provinces and pretend that their various needs and priorities are absolutely non-existent? Quite frankly, I have not made up my mind. I think that hospitals will no longer be able to be just expensive workshops for doctors. I do not think that right now we should put doctors on salary. But there is certainly one thing of which I am convinced: the fee for service principle is not working. Maybe that is the other extreme from salaries. Has there been any intelligent discussion in this House about the extreme of putting doctors on salary? No. Has it happened in committee? No. When we ask officials if they have discussed it, we are told no. Have they consulted the provinces about it? No. Every expert in the field realizes that somewhere between the extreme of fee for service and putting doctors on salary we must work out a viable formula or we will break the bank. Has there been a discussion on that? No. The federal government blocks its ears and is unilaterally confronting the provinces with a cost formula, and goodness knows where they got it.
All I say to the minister is, "Do your homework. Sit down with the provinces. Consult them vis-a-vis hospital regionalization, ambulatory care, the training of paramedical workers, emergency services, community clinics, emphasis on preventive medicine, home care and other clinics." Only when these matters are discussed intelligently-not separating medicare from the hospital services act as members opposite would have us do-then, and only then, will we be taking one of the few initial steps of bringing costs under control.
In the doctorless villages of our rural areas and inner cities we still have money being voted into people's pockets for services that are plainly not there. Low income people in our inner cities, as doctors gravitate to the hospitals, are left with no doctors and no paramedical people to take up the slack, because we have not trained them. They have no ability. It is all very well for those in the ivory towers, who are healed, to say they should have the ability; but the fact is they do not. They often cannot get to hospitals. There are no doctors, there is no ability, no community clinics, no paramedical people. These things are in reports that have been before the government for 20 years. How long do we have to wait?
The best this government can do, after seeing expenditures go from $10 billion to $36 billion, is to confront the provinces with a cost cut. Surely the backbenchers on the government side can make the minister listen. Just because I do not happen to be a member of that party, do not think that I take any delight over this. Let us wake up and get going. I think it creates a lot of cynicism in the body politic, after seeing expenditures go up from $10 billion to $36 billion in eight years, that the first thing you

cut is a centrifugal, pioneer social program before you get at the real cuts.
In conclusion, medical and health care services constitute one of the many challenges which are not being met by federalism as now practised in Canada. Like the challenge of the environment, transportation, living space in our cities, education and the rest, medical and health care services are the very viability of Canadian federalism, something that was alluded to by the hon. member who preceded me. Medicare schemes, as I said before, continue to be merely a finance mechanism. The complete breakdown of service will come about sooner than we care to think. If doctors and medical men will not go into underserviced areas, surely a decent and humane state has an obligation to ensure that medical personnel are equitably distributed.
Public costs mean that public resources should be used to influence the operation of systems that are essential for the health needs of all the people. Costs will continue to skyrocket if government, working with the public and medical profession, does not assume its responsibilities in determining, as I said before, that the plant, personnel and services are made ready. If they are not, I ask this House what the money was voted for in the first place.
Ottawa must give strong central direction and co-ordination to these programs. However, the delivery of modern medical and health care services means a high degree of decentralization, which in turn means responsiveness to local and community needs. Ottawa does not have all the answers. More often, the people in communities know what is best for them and how best to govern their affairs. At the same time, the central authority must assure that local action is carried out in co-operation with other regions, especially when we contemplate hospital regionalization.
To date, Ottawa has not taken into account, especially with the provinces, the principle of local self-agency, forcing the provinces to participate in medicare schemes which in principle are good. Federal authorities are doing next to nothing to permit the provinces, and in turn local government, to have realistic taxing powers to enable them to play their part in any progressive medicare program. The same could be said of the joint hospitalization program. By refusing to help the provinces make the plans, resources and personnel for these programs, Ottawa must share much of the blame for the current nightmare both in the distribution of services and of skyrocketing costs.
If we are serious about providing a better and more equitable distribution of services, especially in the doctorless villages of rural and inner-core urban areas I have already mentioned, immediate action is necessary. More regional clinics will have to be built, together with smaller clinics in local communities. Family health workers will have to be trained to work with doctors and local people. For all paramedical workers a uniform standard of subsidization for training should be implemented, together with a proper quality control supervisory system. This means the successful application of incentives in career planning. Medical schools and hospitals with community and regional responsibilities should have the task of creating a sys-
March 17, 1976

tematic scheme for recruiting, training and deploying paramedical workers.
Sound management and business techniques must be applied to hospitals. These include staff organization and effective communications, meaningful financial reporting, regional planning, effective utilization of manpower and computer technology. If the federal government would only consult with the provinces, it could play a leading part, a pioneer role in effecting a reduction of these problems. Objective criteria must be set up to govern admissions, investigative treatment, length of stay, and discharge. Doctors must realize the financial repercussions of their activities. No longer can we allow hospitals to become doctors' workshops.
Incentives to improve care, reduce costs and increase efficiency must be introduced into the hospital sector in co-operation with the provinces. Administrators, not doctors, must run our hospitals. Trustees and governors should be responsible for over-all policy, and doctors must concentrate upon the practice of medicine. In order to have good hospital administrators, we must provide incentives. In future, regional hospital planning must receive more emphasis as hospitals assume more responsibility toward the particular communities in which they are to be found. A greater number of hospitals must share high-cost facilities.
Hospital admissions will be reduced only when we give due priority to expenditures on preventive medicine, health care clinics, general ambulatory care centres, home care programs, regional community clinics, nursing and convalescent homes and other facilities which could treat and care for patients who now find themselves admitted to general community hospitals. To this extent we cannot discuss medicare in a vacuum apart from hospital insurance, although separate programs, are involved. In the area of discipline and control in relation to hospitals, Ottawa must assume responsibility for adequate staffing, financing and accreditation programs. Peer review and medical auditing must be made meaningful, while medical record procedures are updated through the help of computer technology. Doctors can no longer control their own disciplining and medical associations must become public bodies governed in the interests of the public.
In closing, I should like to ask, in relation to the roles of Ottawa and the provinces vis-a-vis medical and health care services: Where do we go from here? I hope the present debate is the last of its kind, when all we hear from the government is its intention to cut costs in accordance with some incomprehensible formula. I hope the next time we take part in such a discussion we can engage in a substantive debate about the humane and decent delivery of health care services to people at the grass roots level in terms of the planification of plant and personnel.
Lack of public concern and interest is largely responsible for the present mess. An integral part in any advance depends on enlightened public interest and action. As the shroud of mystery is lifted from medical services and activities, questions must be asked and performance demanded by the federal government which transfers so many of the dollars which those services cost. In many ways this is already happening as a result of the information explosion which is taking place in our post-industrial
Medical Care Act
society. Electric communications in general, and television in particular, have brought out and exposed so many problems to public scrutiny. The danger lies in the fact that everything we see, hear or read about seems to constitute a crisis, until we become virtually crisis-immune and can no longer distinguish between bona fide and imaginary problems.
