speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the privilege of speaking a second time on Bill C-68 after helping to open the debate in late January. I promise one thing; I shall not try to copy the act of the last speaker. In my speech in January I covered many aspects of medicare, but there is one in particular I should like to continue to discuss today. I believe that cost efficiency in the program is necessary, that it is possible and that it can be achieved through voluntary means without lowering the level of national health care.
The Ottawa Citizen of March 16-yesterday-had this to say:
Because medicare is a relatively new program, while hospital insurance dates back to the 1950s it is medicare that has been fingered for most of the blame in the dramatic escalation of health costs.
But it is hospital insurance that is responsible for three-quarters of the $8 billion of health costs. Moreover, the hospital insurance bill went up by 25 per cent last year, compared to only 12 per cent for medicare.
This is undebatable and is a point that has been made many times in this debate. More importantly, the Ontario health minister, the Hon. Frank Miller, recently was told in the Ontario legislature that the greatest weakness in the OHIP system is the open-ended arrangement with the Ontario Medical Association. The MLA concerned further stated that there are no incentives in the system for doctors to cut down on unnecessary work. Well, Mr. Speaker, that may be true to some extent, but then Mr. Miller went on to say that methods to close the system are not as foolproof as they appear to be at first glance. He said that the province will try to evolve a closed system of payments for health insurance. I think that is good news for all of us. However, he said that we need to know more about what motivates people and what gives good service than we know now. Those are wise words and deserve to be heeded.
I should just like to digress for a moment in order to comment on one particular aspect of increased hospital costs, and that is nurses' pay. Recently, some hospital spokesmen in Ontario were quoted as saying that high wage settlements awarded to nurses were responsible- they did not say "partly responsible"; they said "responsible"-for the province's spiralling health bill. They said that grade 12 students with two years' community college training can command almost $13,000 a year as nurses, and that they are completely useless. They urged the Ontario government to stand up to the nurses on future wage talks even if it results in a strike. Brave men!
Was it not that very Ontario government that set up the new nursing courses in community colleges and that held nurses' pay down shamefully until recent years? I believe that no reasonable person would regret the increases in nurses' incomes which have been permitted recently, regardless of increasing hospital costs. Our nurses are among the best in the world and deserve every cent of what they are receiving.

I should like to return to my main and previous theme of reducing health care costs through voluntary means by eliminating overservicing, partly through good health maintenance and, therefore, reduced patient demand for medical and hospital care. We may close hospitals and change the rules and facilities of the health care system, but to a large measure what we will always need is the full co-operation and understanding of both doctors and patients.
In regard to patient overdemand, I should like to quote from a small pamphlet, the Medical Review Committee Bulletin, published by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario which is a watchdog organization on Ontario doctors. In a recent issue it carried articles dealing with the physician's responsibility for claims, conflict of interest, billing during the physician's absence, and so on. This is a very responsible group that oversees medical care. The last article in this particular issue carries the heading "Patient demand for unnecessary medical services". This article reads as follows:
The Medical Review Committee has become aware that some physicians are apparently having difficulty in coping with patient demand for excessive and unnecessary medical services. This concern does not address itself to the occasional visit which may be in retrospect unnecessary but rather to the repeated and troublesome demand on the part of some patients for the performance of unnecessary services by the physician.
It is recognized that some physicians may cope with this problem by dismissing the patient from their care; however, some members have expressed a desire to have an opportunity to report the demands of these patients to the proper authority so that the adverse effect upon health care budgeting may be minimized. The Medical Review Committee would advise members of the profession that consultation at the most senior levels of the health insurance plan indicates that the office of the general manager would be most receptive to communication from physicians with respect to the excessive demands made by patients in such unusual cases and would be fully prepared to investigate and attempt to remedy such abuses by patients.
Certainly, a responsible response by doctors to what is often not a responsible approach by patients. I am not attacking the patient population, but they have their faults as much as anyone else and this should be recognized. As far as the doctors are concerned, we have already stated that very heavy demands are made on them and we have documented this. If our doctors are properly distributed and located, they do not need unnecessary work either for their own satisfaction or their personal income. But by the same token they do need to be well looked after.
Let me talk for a moment about the welfare of the doctors themselves. Recently the magazine Canadian Doctor published some interesting facts on the health and welfare of doctors themselves. Dr. M. O. Vincent, executive director of the Homewood sanitorium in Guelph, Ontario, has suggested that doctors should learn to say no to excessive demands on their time and energy. He said more and more Canadian doctors are being treated for mental breakdowns and the incidence is highest among "those who can't say no". He says that emotional ills in physicians often lead to alcoholism and even drug addiction and that these problems are more often observed among doctors than among most other college graduate occupational groups. It was noted that the suicide rate among physicians, especially psychiatrists, is unusually high. Charging that too many other doctors have unrealistic expectations of themselves,
March 17, 1976

he urged them to realize that their time and stamina are limited and to plan their lives accordingly.
The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario has set up a new committee to determine whether physicians are fit enough mentally or physically to practice medicine. This new body could require any physician to submit to a physical or mental examination. Refusal to do so could result in suspension or loss of licence. It will be interesting to see the eventual results of this study. My own experience suggests that the doctor who remains healthiest and happiest may be the family physician in the rural area.
Just a few words, Mr. Speaker, about doctors' incomes. This seems to be one of the main concerns in discussing this medicare bill, along with some smaller administrative costs. What exactly has been the record of doctors' fees and net disposable incomes in recent years? The profession adhered voluntarily to the federal government's wage and guidelines in 1971 under the commission set up by Dr. John Young, and thereby demonstrated considerable economic responsibility right through 1975. During a five-year period in which inflation rose over 30 per cent, Ontario doctors received increases of 4.5 per cent in 1971, 7.75 per cent in 1974 and 4 per cent in 1975, a total of 16.25 per cent.
In real income gains before tax over the past 20 years, a recent survey shows that doctors gained only 38 per cent, the lowest of all 20 groups compared, and only half the Canadian average of 75 per cent. Their position in the group of 20 has even deteriorated in that time from fifteenth place to twentieth, or last. Over the past ten years they have actually lost purchasing power. Their incomes and, therefore, their percentage increases may be among the highest in the country, but that is our system, a hierarchy of incentives and rewards and not a socialistic levelling. That is what has made our system energetic and effective, whereas graduated income tax and social programs also make it humane.
In spite of losing ground economically, the doctors are prepared to co-operate with the anti-inflation program as long as it is applied consistently and fairly; and that, of course, includes the medicare amendments. They would also like to feel their efforts are appreciated, which is probably just as important. In a letter to members of the Canadian Medical Association, dated January 14, 1976, the president, Dr. Lloyd D. Grisdale, stated:
Lastly, as your president, I ask that you honour the commitment made by the C.M.A. to parliament, the government and the people of Canada on behalf of the medical profession. I ask that, for the trial period we promised, you honour the letter and the spirit of the antiinflation legislation of which it forms a major part. The control of inflation is essential. We have a responsibility, as a responsible profession and citizens, to support the decisions and efforts of our duly elected representatives to that end.
The Ottawa Citizen of yesterday wrote:
Before the income controls were introduced, doctors in Ontario and Alberta were calling for 35 per cent hikes in their medicare fee schedules. Faced with the $2,400 annual limit on income gains, they settled for eight and nine per cent respectively.
The problems of the health care system, like all our current problems, need to be worked out, not by confrontation but by consultation between the federal and provincial governments and the health professionals involved.
Medical Care Act
Hopefully, the climate for that constructive approach is developing. Before I close, I should just like to return to one aspect of this subject of health care costs that I touched upon the last time. I want to make a few more comments on the area of the relationship between the increasing cost and the migration of medical doctors to Canada.
Already one-third of Canada's 32,000 doctors are foreign-trained. Perhaps at one time they were needed more than they are now. The professional migration process also contributes to a medical brain-drain undesirable in other countries and they have let us know about this. Redistribution of our own doctors would help the situation, preferably on a voluntary basis. Many people think that the best incentives for doctors to return to the boondocks, as it were, would be higher income and better facilities, whereas it may be that most people these days prefer an urban lifestyle, not only the doctors but their wives and their children as well.
The Ottawa Citizen lead editorial of January 21, 1975, questioned restrictions on the migration of foreign doctors. It expressed doubts as to whether they can be kept in rural areas, but this may in fact not be impossible. It also poked fun at Frank Miller's claim that each additional doctor costs a province $250,000 annually in terms of the health services he generates. However, this can actually happen even in an area where an extra doctor is not strictly needed, and I represent such an area. The potential for expansion of medical services is virtually limitless. Mr. Miller states that these restrictions could save Canada $500 million a year. I think that is very possible and believable. The key questions are: How many doctors do we need? How many can we afford? How can we maximize the opportunities for Canadians to participate? How can we make sure we have the right distribution of such professionals? How can we best look after the welfare of these valuable professional people?
In conclusion, in this sense the federal minister is proposing a series of amendments to Bill C-68, the medicare bill, which should begin to respond to some of the more serious concerns expressed, particularly those expressed by medical people themselves. These proposed amendments are as follows. The exact ceilings are to be set for two years only. Inflation and other factors are too difficult to predict beyond that time. Those ceilings exceed the present anti-inflation guidelines because other expenses may be involved besides payments to doctors. The federal government maintains the option of setting ceilings beyond this two-year period if such are necessary in light of the situation at that time. If the figures have not been stated, it is because they cannot realistically be stated. The method of arriving at these ceilings is subject to full consultation with the provinces.
Second, there will be provision for increases for new important classes of services. Obviously, whatever the cost, a new lifesaving method, for example, is a must and the provinces introducing it deserve to be rewarded accordingly. Third and last, there will be a three-year exemption from the ceiling for new insured services. This will allow a period for build-up and stabilization of initial costs. As I said before, these amendments are designed to help make

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was an acceptable point of order to be interrupted by, but I hope it is not my rising that causes you to leave the chair. In any event, I want to say a few words about the bill before us. This is the first time I have intervened while the medicare bill has been before the House. I do so now because of a number of comments made by hon. members on the other side I think they have been trying to leave the impression with the Canadian people that the cost-sharing formula is not going to be changed and that the provinces, in reality, will be receiving perhaps more money from the federal government than in the past. I suggest there is a bit of deception in that argument being perpetrated by some, though not all, Liberal members across the floor.
In the past there was a cost-sharing agreement under which the federal government paid 50 per cent of the cost of health care in this country. That type of formula will not be adhered to in the future. The type of legislation that is being pushed through the House by this closure or time allocation will limit the increased share of federal participation to 50 per cent plus 13 per cent of the additional costs in the next year. If the costs next year should increase by 14 per cent, 15 per cent or 16 per cent, it will not be a 50-50 cost-sharing arrangement between the provinces and the federal government.

There is a strong likelihood that medical care costs and hospital costs in this country will go up by more than 13 per cent next year. If that is the case, the federal government's share of the total cost of health and medical care in this country will be under 50 per cent. I think that is a retrograde step; it is a step backward from the policy the government has been pursuing in this country for a number of years. I think that point should be made known to the Canadian people, because the government is misleading the House in attempting to say that it will uphold its obligation in the field of medical care. It is not.
It is for this reason that I think the debate before the House is very important. I want to say a few words about that, not just because I come from the province of Saskatchewan where, as you know, Mr. Speaker, CCF and NDP governments pioneered hospitalization and medical care under the premiership of the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), and later under Woodrow Lloyd who succeeded him as premier. This program has since become the norm for medical care and hospitalization in Canada.
In those days there were many tough fights in respect of the principle of universality of medical care. Who was the opposition in those days? I remember well, during the medicare crisis, when the Liberal party, led by the late Ross Thatcher who later became premier, led a group of citizens in opposition to medical care in the province of Saskatchewan. They opposed it in the province with great vigour and determination. Today, after many years of convincing and persuading the federal government about the need for universal medical care where everyone, regardless of financial background, can have the same availability of medical care, we see the federal government taking a retrograde step in gradually backing out of medical care.
I think this party and this House should make sure that every Canadian citizen knows what is happening. This has broad ramifications, not only in respect of medical care but in respect of the way the party on the other side of the House looks at federalism, co-operation and the type of country it wants to create and which I suggest will be created by this type of legislation. The country will be much worse off than it is today.
If we have an increase this year and next year which exceeds the limitations imposed by the government, then the provinces will be faced with a couple of options. The wealthy provinces like Ontario can continue to provide services for their people because they have the financial base with which to do so. Many people in Alberta, Ontario, British Columbia, and perhaps a few other provinces, may not suffer much because of the legislation before the House today. I do not know whether they will or not. They may not, because those provinces have resources they can spend on health care and medicine. But as my colleague from Saskatchewan says, we will do our own thing in Saskatchewan despite the fact that we do not have the wealth and resources of the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia. We did it before.
I alluded to the fight we had with the doctors' committee in Saskatchewan. This was a fight against the first universal medical care plan in North America. The reactionary
March 17, 1976

Liberal party at that time led that fight and said time and time again that they would not rest until medical care was destroyed in the province of Saskatchewan and never came about in Canada. Now we see a retrograde step in this direction.
What will happen in respect of provinces which do not have the same resources as wealthy provinces such as Ontario? What will happen in Newfoundland, in poor little Prince Edward Island, in New Brunswick and in some of the other provinces which cannot afford to put much provincial money into the provision of health services on a par with provinces such as Ontario? These provinces will have to scale down the quality of medicine they provide to their citizens. They do not have any option. The quality of medicine will be scaled down. Its availability will be scaled down. The hospitals and facilities they have will not be expanded because they will not have the necessary funds.
Let us look at a third option which was looked at and adopted by a Liberal government of Saskatchewan. I refer to the imposition of a deterrent fee. That was imposed by the Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan. That is one way to get more money to pay for medical care and hospitalization. I remember the deterrent fee very well. That was back in the days of the late premier Ross Thatcher in the province of Saskatchewan.
I remember those days well because that was the time I really became active in politics, in the mid-1960s, when I saw fees of $2 and $2.50 being imposed on people who visited a doctor. Who are the people involved? They are the people least able to afford to pay doctors' bills-the older people and those with large families. They are the people who cannot afford it. The Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan brought in the deterrent fee, or the usury fee. I think that is a very regressive way in which to finance any plan, particularly a plan such as this which should be universally acceptable to everyone.
I believe medical care should be free to everyone. I do not mean simply the type of care we have today. I include pharmacare through which people who need drugs could get them at cost. I include denticare. Dental care should be provided to everyone regardless of income. I also refer to the provision of hearing aids and everything else people need for their physical well-being or care. That will not happen if this bill should pass.
If the federal government starts to scale down the amount of money it provides in respect of medical care and hospitalization, the provinces will not be able to extend or expand the services they want to provide to the citizens of this country. That is the reason we oppose this bill and will fight it as strongly as we can. It seems to me that whenever we oppose something on principle, the government says that we are being obstructionist, that we are carrying on a filibuster, or we are trying to obstruct the legislation. Then, as in this case, they bring in closure. If the government wants co-operation from the opposition, the last thing it should do is introduce closure or time allocation. The government should be open to amendments, because I think in this case, like in the case in which we have been involved in the last few days, it is the opposition parties that are sensitive to the feelings of the people.
I think the government opposite will not be there for many more months. I think the government is marking
Medical Care Act
time. I think this is another example of a government that has had too much power for too long. It is too arrogant. Can you tell me, Mr. Speaker, of any province which agrees with the type of proposal being brought down by the Minister' of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde)? We have NDP provinces, one Social Credit province, and Liberal and Conservative provinces. What about Premier Reagan of Nova Scotia; what does he think about the bill which is before us today?
What about Robert Bourassa in Quebec? Why is the federal government interested in curtailing health costs, and why is the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) asking where we should cut? If the government is interested in cutting, why does it not talk to the provinces and work something out on a bilateral basis? Why is the federal government, instead, bringing in a bill in a unilateral and authoritarian way? That is not the way to govern this country. That is going back.
This Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has talked like a university professor conducting a philosophical class about how we should govern, what kind of country we should have and what kind of federal union we should have. I do not mind making the charge that I think this Prime Minister has done more to provoke disunity in this country than any other prime minister in the history of Canada. I suggest there is more disunity now than there ever has been in this country.
Recently I spent a few days in the province of Quebec. I was surprised that almost all the people I spoke to criticized the federal Prime Minister for the attitude he took toward the Prime Minister of Quebec. I found this criticism also in the journals I read, and I heard it in the commentaries. It is this type of heavy-handed attitude which this government has taken for far too long on almost every issue before us to which I object.

I am writing as a member of the board of the Atlantic Research Centre for Mental Retardation to express my concern about the current financial squeeze on medical research in this country, particularly as it relates to the Atlantic Research Centre for mental retardation, Halifax, N.S. Canada's expenditure per capita for medical research, when compared with that of other western nations, is disgracefully low.
I am just quoting from the letter. I do not know whether the facts are correct. The letter goes on:

I am sure that every Canadian medical scientist is prepared to do his or her utmost to co-operate in fighting inflation-but only if scientists

receive treatment comparable to labour unions. I therefore urge that the government reconsider its regrettable action in this matter.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may speak to the minister's point of order, I suggest that my colleague for Northwest Territories and I enjoy the distinction, if you look at it that way, of being unique in this House. Whereas other members of the House represent constituencies in provinces, and a provincial body may interpose itself between the federal government and the people of the province, the hon. member for Northwest Territories and I must deal directly with the federal government. Therefore, I am saying now those things which would be said if we were given a voice at federal-provincial conferences. But we are not given that voice and are not allowed to say these things. This House is the only forum in which we can present certain views.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Come to my estimates.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: I enjoy attending when the minister's estimates are discussed, but that does not help elected representatives of the people of the Yukon in their deliberations in the legislative assembly. That process does not allow them to provide input to the minister's decisions. I submit that what I say is pertinent to the bill, to moneys being spent on medicare and the manner in which they are spent. Allow me to cite one more example. The government was not satisfied with leaving matters there. It looked for the most prominent person it could find in the Yukon in order to make an example of him in the enforcement of the medicare law. Who did it find?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
That is right, the hon. member for Yukon, as the minister knows. So they charged him. Where could he go for good, sound advice? He was tried and convicted of failing to register for medicare. What did the hon. member for Yukon do? He obtained the best legal advice he could-from the then minister of justice who now is Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). The then minister of justice said, "That is silly. Saskatchewan has a medicare scheme but I belong to the Ontario scheme. Why can you not belong to the scheme to which I belong?" The minister belonged to one scheme for 19 years. At that I appealed and the appeal court reversed the decision. That is an example of the government's heavy-handed methods, to use the

phrase used by the NDP member who last spoke, in enforcing medicare in the Yukon.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: It's a good thing you didn't see a judge.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Now I shall pass to something more serious. I am enjoying the debate and do not wish to change the tone. Nevertheless, what I shall now raise has a direct bearing on matters being discussed in the House. One of the minister's employees in northern health services, Dr. Connolly, felt it was wrong of the city of Whitehorse to continue dumping raw sewage into the Yukon River from a sewage system designed, installed and paid for by the federal government and then handed to the city of Whitehorse. He laid a charge against the city of Whitehorse under a medical health ordinance in the Yukon. Dr. Connolly then was acting as medical health officer for the Yukon but was an employee of the minister's department.
He was telephoned by someone in the commissioner's office, the commissioner's office being under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), and was told, "Withdraw that charge." Dr. Connolly, more credit to him, said, "No, sir, I will not withdraw the charge. An offence has been committed and it will be proceeded with." There was a series of telephone calls from the commissioner's office, culminating with this message, "Either you withdraw the charge or I will communicate with my minister, who will communicate with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who will require you to withdraw the charge. If you do not comply, you will be fired."
According to my information, all communications were beneath ministerial level: the ministers personally were not involved; the officials were. As it happened, there was a telephone communication from the commissioner's office to the office of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, hence to the office of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It went back down to regional office in Edmonton and back up to Dr. Connolly in Whitehorse. He was told, "You will either withdraw the charge and say publicly that the matter is proceeding satisfactorily and that is why you are withdrawing the charge, or you will be fired." The minister shakes his head, but he does not know this because he was not there personally.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Were you there?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Hon. members will agree, surely, that that is unacceptable pressure. I was told this by Dr. Connolly. There is no better source. Section 127 (2) of the Criminal Code provides:
Every one who wilfully attempts in any manner other than a manner described in subsection (1) to obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for ten years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Was he fired?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
I agree that if pressure had been brought to bear on Dr. Connolly before the charge was laid, there would be no difficulty. But after the charge was laid and placed in the hands of the Crown attorney, pressure was brought to bear on Dr. Connolly. He was threatened with loss of his job if he did not withdraw. At that stage he
March 17, 1976

threw up his hands and said, "I will not press charges." By that time the matter was in the hands of the Crown attorney. I am not suggesting for a moment that the Department of Justice brought pressure to bear on the Crown attorney. Even if it did, I have such high regard for him that I know he would not succumb. Nonetheless, there was communication to determine if there was sufficient evidence. There was evidence and the charge proceeded. A fine of $100 was the result.
I maintain that the circumstances I have disclosed are serious enough to warrant investigation. It is not my job or the job of any other member to judge guilt or innocence. But it is the government's responsibility to investigate the matter to see if there is a prima facie case for a charge to be laid under section 127 of the Criminal Code. If it is deemed that there is sufficient evidence to support a prima facie case under section 127, the government should see to it that every official of government involved in bringing pressure to bear is charged under the section. Let the courts decide guilt or innocence.
Message from the Senate
I see that my time has almost expired. May I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate informing this House that the Senate have passed Bill C-71, an act to amend the Criminal Code and to make related amendments to the Crown Liability Act, the Immigration Act and the Parole Act, with amendments, to which the concurrence of this House is desired.
At 6.01 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
